A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPMARL research work. Their text, equations, figures and tables are readable and support comparison. v2 ends with references and has no separate appendix; v3 includes Appendix A, which was included in the assessment.

before.justification: v2 reports original training, evaluation and generated-curriculum results for Simple-Spread, 10-player XOR and SMAC-v2 Protoss 5 versus 5 in Figures 3, 5 and 7.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark experiments, objective-variance comparisons and threshold ablations in the main text and Appendix A, including Figures 4–11 and Tables 1–2.

M1.justification: Both retain critic-loss prioritization, two-stage KL-constrained curriculum updates, shared-policy MAPPO and discretized Gaussian agent counts. v2 Equations 8–9 match v3 Equations 4–5. SPRL is renamed SPRLM; the expanded TD-error explanation does not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: v3 replaces the 10-player XOR target with 20 players, adds Protoss 6v6, 7v7 and 8v8, and adds Terran and Zerg 5v5/6v6 experiments. Appendix A.3.3 further introduces dense-reward Balance and Wheel tasks, substantially extending coverage beyond v2's three sparse-reward scenarios.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated ALPGMM and adaptive VACL comparators to the main benchmark comparisons and removes Random. v2 cited VACL but represented prior multi-agent curricula through Linear rather than evaluating this adaptive comparator. SPRL/SPRLM and Linear remain; W/O Teacher remains evaluated in Table 1 despite being omitted from the plots.

E3.justification: The evaluation axes change from environment steps to environment samples proportional to agent count, changing the reported sample-efficiency accounting. v3 also introduces performance summaries averaged during training and controlled VLB sweeps. General VLB guidance changes from the expected target return to approximately 80% of it, although Simple-Spread's explicitly stated threshold of 50 remains.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's descriptive analysis of training and curriculum curves, v3 directly compares objective dispersion across six tasks in Figures 7 and 10. It also adds VLB sensitivity experiments on Protoss 5v5 and 6v6 in Figure 11, providing previously absent evidence about the proposed mechanism and hyperparameter robustness.

E5.justification: The Simple-Spread statement of five seeds and 95% confidence intervals is retained. v3 adds mean/standard-deviation summaries and one-sided Mann–Whitney U tests across the six main tasks in Tables 1–2, plus an explicit objective-dispersion estimator in Appendix A.3.4. No increase in seed count is stated.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for new tasks, comparators, variance comparisons and threshold sweeps. Table 1 newly reports training-averaged Simple-Spread performance of 33.36 (SD 1.84) for SPMARL versus 27.48 (SD 5.38) for SPRLM; larger Protoss tasks reveal weak SPRLM performance. The 20-player XOR results replace 10-player results, so they do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: The core Dec-POMDP, contextual-RL, MAPPO/GAE and curriculum-optimization mathematics is retained, with MAPPO moved to Appendix A.2. No new theorem, proof or formal guarantee is introduced. The added standard-deviation formula and TD-target explanation document the empirical analysis.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain agent-number curricula and critic-loss-based SPMARL. v3 makes high-variance return estimation a headline problem in the abstract and conclusion, and qualifies SPRLM's success as applying to most tasks rather than v2's consistent-success statement. These refine the claims without redefining the approach.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking ALPGMM/VACL performance to failure to converge to the target distribution and attributing SPRLM's larger-Protoss failures to sparse-return optimization. Appendix A.3.3 adds an applicability qualification: dense rewards reduce exploration challenges and curriculum benefits. v2's Random-prior discussion is removed; the unresolved necessity of the KL constraint remains.

D1.justification: v2 largely provides qualitative implementation guidance and refers readers to code. v3 adds Tables 3–8 specifying network, optimizer, rollout, episode-length and curriculum-distribution settings, including task-specific thresholds. The code pointer changes from anonymous hosting to a named GitHub repository. These are primarily additional disclosures, not evidence that all underlying settings changed.

R1.justification: v3 adds ALPGMM-related literature, a comparison with prioritized experience replay, brief connections to unsupervised environment design and numerical continuation, and newer MARL and benchmark references. The principal positioning relative to SPRL and existing agent-number curricula remains intact; the PORTAL entry is updated to its published version.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanations and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting. Background becomes Problem Formulation, SPRL and SPMARL receive separate sections, and MAPPO and implementation material move into the appendix. SPRLM terminology, organized supplementary sections, acknowledgements and an impact statement further restructure the document.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main text, redraws Figure 1, and combines the XOR payoff matrix and SMAC illustration into Figure 3. Benchmark plots have revised axes, legends and expanded panel grids. New statistical and hyperparameter tables, variance plots and ablation figures substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves validation and reproducibility through direct ALPGMM/VACL comparisons, broader task coverage, sensitivity and statistical analyses, and explicit experimental settings in Tables 3–8. The dense-reward experiments also clarify where benefits diminish. Removing Random loses some comparison coverage, and Table 2 does not establish superiority in every comparison, but the added evidence makes the paper's effectiveness and limitations substantially more assessable.
